A Technical Glance

This repository contains the framework and configuration for generating a static documentation site deployed at wisconsin.twango.dev.

The setup is Obsidian-compatible, allowing you to edit notes locally in Obsidian while maintaining version control through Git and automated deployments for web access. This creates a seamless workflow for note-taking, version control, and sharing.

TIP

This setup excels for CS students - keep notes and code together in one repository. Works seamlessly with AI assistants (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf) that benefit from having full project context.

WARNING

Academic Compliance: All course materials remain in private submodules to comply with academic policies. This public repository contains only the site framework—no assignments, solutions, or proprietary content are exposed. The deployed site is access-controlled to protect course content.

Bonus Features

This Quartz instance has been enhanced with several custom features tailored for students and course content management:

  • Automatic Tagging System: Intelligently generates tags from directory structure (course codes, terms, subjects)
  • Scope-Based Tag Application: Course tags apply globally while term/subject tags target immediate content only
  • Smart Title Extraction: Automatically uses H1 headings as page titles with special handling for README files
  • Centered Math Equations: KaTeX display equations are automatically centered for better readability
  • Consistent Image Layout: Article images display at 60% width with balanced margins
  • Improved Frontmatter Processing: Intelligent title fallback system
  • Multi-threaded Parsing: Dynamically uses all available CPU cores for faster build times

Scaling

This project was designed to scale to contain content for multiple courses or semesters. You should consider using Git submodules to keep content organized and access controlled

Benefits of this approach:

  • Privacy: Keep sensitive course materials in private repositories
  • Modularity: Each course can be managed independently with its own commit history
  • Selective Sharing: Share only specific courses by making individual submodules public
  • Performance: Clone only the content you need instead of the entire repository
  • Collaboration: Different people can maintain different course repositories

Deployment

Quartz generates static files in public/ that can be deployed anywhere:

Hosting Options: GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel, AWS S3/Cloudflare R2, the CSL or any static file server.

Access Control: Since Quartz outputs static HTML, implement authentication at the infrastructure level:

  • Cloudflare Zero Trust, Authentik, or Pangolin for identity-based access
  • Basic Auth via web server configuration
  • Edge functions for custom authorization logic

This approach keeps your site fast while protecting sensitive course materials.

  • Author information

Question 3 (? points)

Write either “True” or “False” for each of the questions below. If you answer “False” give an explanation or show how to change the statement into a true statement.

The following code will be referenced for these questions.

Assume: i_array is held in the register %esi and c_array is in the register %edi Note: sizeof(int) is 4 and sizeof(char) is 1.

(A) i_array[5] and *(i_array+5) is equivalent.

  • True
  • False

Answer (A)

Correct: True

Array indexing a[i] is defined as *(a+i) in C — they are exactly equivalent.

(B) *ip = i_array is a valid C statement.

  • True
  • False

Answer (B)

Correct: False

ip is an int * and i_array decays to int *. You cannot assign a pointer to a dereferenced pointer with *ip = i_array; that would try to store an address into an int. The correct form would be ip = i_array (make ip point to the array).

(C) The following x86 statements will load the 5th element of i_array (e.g., i_array[5] in C) into %eax.

  • True
  • False

Answer (C)

Correct: False

The scale factor should be 4 (since sizeof(int) == 4), not 1. The correct instruction is movl (%esi, %ecx, 4), %eax. With scale=1 this reads i_array[1] (offset 5 bytes = byte 5, not element 5).

(D) The following x86 statements will load the 5th element of c_array (e.g., c_array[5] in C) into %eax.

  • True
  • False

Answer (D)

Correct: True

sizeof(char) == 1, so the scale factor of 1 is correct. (%edi, %ecx, 1) computes %edi + 5*1 = c_array + 5, which is c_array[5].

(E) array[11] is a valid C statement (Hint: Trick question?).

  • True
  • False

Answer (E)

Correct: True (trick question)

C does not perform automatic bounds checking. array[11] is syntactically valid and will compile. It accesses memory beyond the array’s bounds (undefined behavior at runtime), but C treats it as valid syntax — the compiler will not reject it.

(F) The four segments of memory provided every executable program are: Heap, Queue, Data, and Code.

  • True
  • False

Answer (F)

Correct: False

The four segments are Stack, Heap, Data (initialized/uninitialized), and Code (text). There is no “Queue” segment. The stack holds local variables and return addresses; the heap is for dynamic allocation.

Time: 75 minutes Total Points: 70 Total Questions: 70

Exam Assumptions

  • The OS manages a single uniprocessor (single core).
  • All memory is byte addressable.
  • The terminology lg means log2.
  • 1 byte = 8 bits.
  • 1 hexadecimal digit takes 4 bits.
  • Page table entries require 4 bytes unless otherwise stated.
  • Data is allocated with optimal alignment, starting at the beginning of a page.
  • Leading zeros can be removed from numbers (e.g., 0x06 == 0x6).
  • Hex numbers are represented with a preceding “0x”; numbers without 0x are decimal.

Part 1: CPU Virtualization Short Answers

Question 1 (1 point)

Which of these are not application benefits of an operating system?

  • A set of simpler abstractions against which to program
  • Independence from specific hardware and devices
  • More control over how hardware is used

Answer

Correct: More control over how hardware is used

Question 2 (1 point)

Which of these are user benefits of an operating system?

  • Protecting running programs against the misbehavior of other programming
  • More physical memory available to programs
  • Sharing hardware by running multiple programs at the same time
  • A & C
  • All the above

Answer

Correct: A & C

Question 3 (1 point)

Which of the following is not a valid process state

  • Blocked
  • Ready
  • Preempting
  • Waiting

Answer

Correct: Preempting

Question 4 (1 point)

Processes are a stream of execution and execution state

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: True

Question 5 (1 point)

The state of a process is its execution state (registers) and memory state

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

The state of a process is just its execution state (CPU registers). Memory state (address space contents) is part of the process’s address space, but the process state that the OS saves/restores is the register set, not the memory contents.

Question 6 (1 point)

Which of the following are present in processes but not programs

  • Stack & registers
  • Heap & data
  • Code & registers
  • Data & code

Answer

Correct: Stack & registers

Question 7 (1 point)

With direct execution, the operating system can take control of the CPU at any time

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

With direct execution (no limited direct execution mechanisms), the OS has no way to regain control. It needs timer interrupts (limited direct execution) to preempt processes.

Question 8 (1 point)

It is not safe to let user-mode code enable and disable interrupts

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: True

Question 9 (1 point)

What does a processor do if a process executes a privileged instruction in user mode?

  • The processor traps
  • The instruction is ignored
  • The computer reboots

Answer

Correct: The processor traps

Question 10 (1 point)

Which of the following are operations allowed in user-mode execution?

  • Access to all areas of physical memory
  • Saving/restoring registers
  • Issuing input/output commands
  • Modifying processor memory management state

Answer

Correct: Saving/restoring registers

Question 11 (1 point)

On a timer interrupt, the hardware is responsible for transitioning from user to kernel mode.

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: True

Question 12 (1 point)

Processes can move from the running state directly to the blocked state

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: True

Question 13 (1 point)

Processes can’t move from the blocked state directly to the ready state

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

Processes can move from blocked directly to ready when their I/O completes.

Question 14 (1 point)

Only one process can be in the RUNNING state

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: True

Question 15 (1 point)

With cooperating multitasking, context switches only happen when a program calls yield()

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

Context switches can also happen on other system calls, process termination, or illegal operations.

Question 16 (1 point)

On a timer interrupt, the operating system always context switches to a new process

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

Question 17 (1 point)

On a context switch, user-mode registers are saved in the process-control block (PCB)

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

On a context switch, user-mode registers are saved on the kernel stack of the process, not the PCB. The PCB stores higher-level process metadata (state, PID, etc.). During a system call, registers are also saved on the kernel stack.

Question 30 (1 point)

For this schedule using FIFO, what is the average turnaround time?

JobLengthArrival

  • Between 3-4 ms

Part 3: Memory Virtualization Short Answers

Question 36 (1 point)

For a single sequential pass over data, a 4-entry TLB performs better than a 1-entry TLB

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

For sequential access, you only access one page at a time before moving to the next. A 1-entry TLB is sufficient.

Question 37 (1 point)

To translate a virtual address using paging, the MMU adds the offset to the physical page number from the TLB

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

The MMU concatenates the physical page number with the offset, it does not add them.

Question 38 (1 point)

With multi-level page tables, larger pages lead to fewer levels in the page table

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: True

Question 39 (1 point)

A process can’t access the data of another process because the other process’s addresses are marked invalided in the page table.

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

Each process has its own page table mapping virtual addresses to different physical addresses. Protection comes from separate page tables, not from marking other process’s addresses as invalid.

Question 40 (1 point)

Which mechanism provides the least protection?

  • Static relocation
  • Base and bounds
  • Segments
  • Paging

Answer

Correct: Static relocation

Question 41 (1 point)

Which mechanism has the least wasted memory for a standard process layout?

  • Segments
  • Base and bounds
  • Paging with linear page tables

Answer

Correct: Segments

Question 42 (1 point)

Which mechanisms support sharing?

  • Segments
  • Paging
  • Paging and base/bounds
  • Base/bounds and segments
  • Segments and paging

Answer

Correct: Segments and paging

Question 43 (1 point)

What is the major benefit of paging over segmentation?

  • Less wasted memory
  • Faster performance
  • Less external fragmentation
  • Less MMU state

Answer

Correct: Less external fragmentation

Question 44 (1 point)

With segmentation, the address space of each process must be allocated contiguously in physical memory

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

Each segment must be contiguous, but different segments can be placed in different locations in physical memory.

Question 45 (1 point)

Compared to using segments, using a 2-level page table with no TLB doubles the number of memory references

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

With segments: 1 memory reference (data access). With a 2-level page table and no TLB: 3 memory references (2 page table lookups + data access). It triples, not doubles.

Question 46 (1 point)

When the dirty bit is set in a PTE, it means the contents of a TLB entry do not match the page table

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

The dirty bit means the page has been written to, not that TLB and page table entries are mismatched.

Question 47 (1 point)

When using paging, larger pages causes more external fragmentation

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

Paging does not have external fragmentation. Larger pages cause more internal fragmentation.

Question 48 (1 point)

To use huge pages (such as 2mb pages), a programmer always has to request them when allocating memory

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

The OS can use huge pages transparently (e.g., transparent huge pages).

Question 49 (1 point)

With shared memory, processes map the same physical pages to the same virtual addresses in multiple processes

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

Shared memory maps the same physical pages, but the virtual addresses can be different in each process.

Question 50 (1 point)

FIFO page replacement always has more page faults than LRU page replacement

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

Question 51 (1 point)

An LRU TLB replacement policy is better than a random TLB replacement policy for sequential workloads.

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

For sequential workloads, old pages are never revisited, so LRU provides no benefit over random.

Question 52 (1 point)

With a software-filled TLB, the OS specifies the layout of the page table

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: True

Question 53 (1 point)

With ASIDs, there is no performance penalty for context switching when using a TLB

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

ASIDs (Address Space Identifiers) tag TLB entries with process IDs so the TLB does not need to be flushed on context switch — this greatly reduces the penalty. However, there is still some performance overhead: the switching process itself, potential TLB contention, and cold-start misses for the new process’s entries not yet in the TLB.

Question 54 (1 point)

When the present bit is cleared in a PTE, accessing the associated page will cause a segmentation fault

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

It causes a page fault, not a segmentation fault.

Question 55 (1 point)

Demand paging never loads at the data at an address referenced by a process before it is used the first time

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

Demand paging loads a page only when it is first accessed (on a page fault). However, modern OS implementations often use prefetching or clustering — when a page fault occurs, the OS may load additional nearby pages anticipating future access. So demand paging does not guarantee that data is never loaded before first use; pure demand paging would, but real systems commonly prefetch.

Question 56 (1 point)

When a system is thrashing, the CPU is fully utilized

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

During thrashing, the CPU is mostly idle waiting for I/O from constant page faults.

Question 57 (1 point)

With inverted page tables, every physical page in a system has a PTE

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: True

Question 58 (1 point)

Copy-on-write is faster than regular copy when a process reads from most of the copied pages.

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: True

COW avoids copying pages that are only read, making it faster when most pages are not written to.

Question 59 (1 point)

If the clock hand in clock page replacement is moving quickly, it could mean

  • The program has high locality
  • The program has low locality

Answer

Correct: The program has low locality

Question 60 (1 point)

With clock page replacement, a page that is marked dirty always has the referenced bit set

  • True
  • False

Answer

Correct: False

The clock algorithm can clear the reference bit during a sweep while the dirty bit remains set.

Question 61 (1 point)

Given a 4 entry TLB and 4KB pages, what will the TLB miss rate be for the line of code shown in boldface?

  • Between 0 and 1%
  • Between 1 and 5 %
  • Between 5 and 10%
  • Between 10 and 25%
  • Higher than 25%

Answer

Correct: Between 0 and 1%

Sequential access. 4KB pages hold 512 doubles (4096/8). Miss rate = 1/512 ≈ 0.2%.

Question 62 (1 point)

Consider this variation of the code. Given a 4 entry TLB and 4KB pages, what will the TLB miss rate be for the line of code shown in boldface?

  • Between 5 and 10%

  • Higher than 25%

Answer

Correct: Higher than 25%

Stride access jumps 1024 elements (8192 bytes = 2 pages) each iteration. With a 4-entry TLB, nearly every access is a miss.

Question 63 (1 point)

Using the same variation of the code from the previous question, consider a system with a 16 entry TLB and 2MB pages. What is the TLB miss rate for the line of code in boldface when running this loop many times?

  • Between 1 and 5 %
  • Between 5 and 10%
  • Between 10 and 25%
  • Higher than 25%

Answer

Correct: Between 0 and 1 %

Array is 8MB = 4 pages of 2MB. All 4 pages fit in a 16-entry TLB. After initial compulsory misses, the miss rate approaches 0%.

Question 64 (1 point)

Given a virtual address size of 32 bits and a page size of 256 bytes and a PTE size of 4 bytes, what is the size of a linear page table?

  • 4MB
  • 16MB
  • 64MB
  • 256MB

Answer

Correct: 64MB

Number of pages = 2^32 / 2^8 = 2^24. Page table size = 2^24 × 4 = 2^26 = 64MB.

Given a virtual address size of 32 bits and a page size of 256 bytes and a PTE size of 4 bytes, how many levels of page table are needed?

  • 3
  • 4

Answer

Correct: 4

PTEs per page = 256/4 = 64 = 2^6. VPN bits = 24. Levels = 24/6 = 4.

Question 66 (1 point)

  • 5

Correct: 7

4-level page table. Code/data/heap at low addresses need 1 page per level (3 pages + 1 root). Stack at top of address space needs a separate page at levels 2-4 (3 pages). Total = 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 7.

Critical Priority Topics

Lecture 15 & Lecture 16: Convolutional Neural Networks

Why Critical: CNN calculations appear on every final exam with heavy computational problems.

Exam Weight: ~25% of questions

Key Concepts:

Convolution Operations:

  • 2D Convolution: Slide kernel across input, compute element-wise products and sum
  • Output size formula: output=⌊sn−k+2p​⌋+1 where n = input size, k = kernel size, p = padding, s = stride
  • Multi-channel convolution: Each filter has depth matching input channels
  • Parameter counting:
    • Per filter: (kh​×kw​×channels)+1 (bias)
    • Total: (filter params)×num filters

Pooling Layers:

  • Max pooling: Take maximum value in each window
  • Average pooling: Take average value in each window
  • No learnable parameters in pooling layers
  • Purpose: Reduce spatial dimensions, provide translation invariance

CNN Advantages over MLPs:

  • Locality: Nearby pixels share structure
  • Translation invariance: Features detected regardless of position
  • Parameter sharing: Same kernel applied across entire image
  • Fewer parameters: More efficient than fully connected layers

CNN Architectures:

  • LeNet: Early CNN for digit recognition
  • AlexNet: Deeper network, ReLU activations, dropout
  • VGG: Very deep (16-19 layers), small 3x3 kernels
  • ResNet: Residual connections to enable very deep networks

Exam Focus Areas:

  • Convolution output calculations (very common!)
  • Parameter counting in convolutional layers
  • CNN vs. MLP comparisons
  • Pooling operations
  • Understanding architecture advantages

Practice Problems:

  • Spring 2024: Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4
  • Spring 2025: Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5
  • Deep Learning Practice Q1-Q7

Lecture 16 & Lecture 17: ResNets and Deep Learning Challenges

Why Critical: Vanishing gradients and residual networks frequently tested.

Exam Weight: ~10% of questions

Key Concepts:

Vanishing Gradient Problem:

  • Gradients become very small in deep networks
  • Makes training deep networks difficult
  • Caused by repeated multiplication of small gradients

Solutions to Vanishing Gradients:

  • ReLU activation: Gradient is 1 for positive inputs (vs. sigmoid’s small gradients)
  • Residual connections: Allow gradients to flow directly through skip connections
  • Batch normalization: Normalizes layer inputs to prevent extreme values
  • NOT: Adding more layers, larger learning rates, more data

Residual Networks (ResNets):

  • Skip connections: Output = F(x)+x
  • Learning residuals: Network learns F(x)=H(x)−x instead of H(x)
  • Easier to learn identity: If optimal is identity, F(x)=0 is easier to learn
  • No additional parameters: Skip connections add paths, not parameters

Data Augmentation:

  • Artificially expand training data through transformations
  • Valid augmentations: Rotation, flipping, cropping, color changes
  • Invalid augmentations: Those that change the label (e.g., flipping “6” to “9”)
  • Domain-specific considerations required

Exam Focus Areas:

  • Identifying solutions to vanishing gradients
  • Understanding residual connections
  • When data augmentation helps vs. hurts
  • Recognizing overfitting scenarios

Practice Problems:

  • Spring 2024: Q5, Q6, Q7, Q8, Q9
  • Spring 2025: Q6, Q7, Q8

Lecture 20: Informed Search (A* Search)

Why Critical: A* search and heuristics appear on every final exam.

Exam Weight: ~15% of questions

Key Concepts:

A Search:*

  • Uses f(n)=g(n)+h(n)
    • g(n): Actual cost from start to node n
    • h(n): Heuristic estimate from n to goal
  • Data structure: Priority queue ordered by f(n)
  • Complete and optimal (with admissible heuristic)

Admissible Heuristics:

  • Definition: h(n)≤h∗(n) for all nodes (never overestimates)
  • h∗(n) is the true cost to goal
  • Properties of admissible heuristics:
    • h(n)=0 is always admissible (but uninformative)
    • h(n)=c⋅h0​(n) where 0<c≤1 and h0​ admissible ⇒ admissible
    • h0​(n)​ is admissible if h0​ is admissible
    • h0​(n)−c may NOT be admissible (could go negative)
    • h0​(n)+c is NOT admissible

Dominating Heuristics:

  • h2​ dominates h1​ if h1​(s)≤h2​(s)≤h∗(s) for all s
  • Prefer dominating heuristic: More accurate, expands fewer nodes

Uniform Cost Search (UCS):

  • Special case of A* with h(n)=0
  • Data structure: Priority queue ordered by g(n)
  • Complete and optimal

Iterative Deepening Search (IDS):

  • Combines DFS space efficiency with BFS completeness
  • Repeatedly runs depth-limited DFS with increasing limits
  • Note: BFS and DFS themselves are excluded, but IDS may still appear

Exam Focus Areas:

  • A search trace calculations*
  • Determining if heuristics are admissible
  • Comparing informed vs. uninformed search
  • Understanding completeness and optimality

Practice Problems:

  • Spring 2024: Q10, Q11, Q12, Q16
  • Spring 2025: Q10, Q11, Q12, Q13
  • Search Practice Q1-Q11

Lecture 21 & Lecture 22: Game Theory

Why Critical: Game theory fundamentals tested on every final.

Exam Weight: ~15% of questions

Key Concepts:

Normal Form Games:

  • Payoff matrix representation
  • Two players, simultaneous moves
  • Payoffs written as (P1​,P2​)

Dominant Strategies:

  • Strictly dominant: Strategy s is strictly dominant if it gives higher payoff than any other strategy, regardless of opponent’s action
  • Dominant Strategy Equilibrium: Both players have dominant strategies
  • To find: Compare payoffs for each action across all opponent actions

Nash Equilibrium (Pure Strategy):

  • No player can improve payoff by unilaterally changing strategy
  • Finding NE: For each cell, check if either player would deviate
  • A dominant strategy equilibrium is always a Nash equilibrium
  • Not every Nash equilibrium is a dominant strategy equilibrium

Minimax Algorithm:

  • For two-player zero-sum sequential games
  • MAX player: Maximizes score (picks max of children)
  • MIN player: Minimizes score (picks min of children)
  • Leaf nodes: Game tree size = bm (branching factor b, depth m)
  • Time complexity: O(bm)

Game Trees:

  • Counting nodes: Sum of nodes at each level
  • Leaf nodes only: bm
  • All nodes: ∑i=0m​bi

Exam Focus Areas:

  • Finding dominant strategies from payoff matrices
  • Identifying Nash equilibria
  • Minimax tree traversal
  • Counting nodes in game trees

Practice Problems:

  • Spring 2024: Q17, Q18, Q19, Q20
  • Spring 2025: Q14, Q15, Q30

Lecture 23: Reinforcement Learning

Why Critical: RL concepts and calculations heavily tested.

Exam Weight: ~15% of questions

Key Concepts:

Markov Decision Process (MDP):

  • Components: States S, Actions A, Transition P(s′∣s,a), Reward R(s) or R(s,a), Discount γ
  • Markov property: Next state depends only on current state and action (not history)

Value Iteration: Vt+1​(s)=r(s)+γmaxa​∑s′​P(s′∣s,a)Vt​(s′)

Key calculation steps:

  1. For each action, compute expected future value: ∑s′​P(s′∣s,a)V(s′)
  2. Take max over actions
  3. Multiply by discount factor γ
  4. Add immediate reward r(s)

Q-Learning: Q(s,a)←Q(s,a)+α[r+γmaxa′​Q(s′,a′)−Q(s,a)]

  • Model-free: Doesn’t need transition probabilities
  • Off-policy: Can learn from any experience

ϵ-Greedy Exploration:

  • With probability 1−ϵ: Choose action with highest Q-value (exploit)
  • With probability ϵ: Choose random action (explore)
  • Balances exploration and exploitation

Discount Factor γ:

  • γ close to 0: Agent cares more about immediate rewards (present)
  • γ close to 1: Agent cares more about future rewards
  • 0<γ<1 ensures convergence

Exam Focus Areas:

  • Value iteration calculations (very common!)
  • Understanding discount factor effects
  • Q-learning update rule
  • ϵ-greedy policy behavior
  • Markov property questions

Common Pitfalls to Avoid

CNN Calculations

  1. Output size formula:

    • Don’t forget the +1 at the end
    • Remember to floor the result
    • Padding adds to BOTH sides: use 2p in formula

  2. Parameter counting:

    • Include biases! Each filter has one bias
    • Kernel depth must match input channels
    • Formula: (kh​×kw​×cin​+1)×num filters

  3. Pooling layers:

    • No learnable parameters
    • Max pooling is NOT linear
    • Average pooling IS linear

A* Search

  1. Admissible heuristics:

    • Must NEVER overestimate true cost
    • h(n)=0 is always admissible
    • Adding a constant makes it inadmissible
    • Subtracting could make it negative (inadmissible)

  2. A trace:*

    • Update fringe with f=g+h
    • Always expand node with lowest f

Game Theory

  1. Dominant strategies:

    • Compare across ALL opponent actions
    • Must be better in EVERY case for strictly dominant

  2. Nash equilibrium:

    • Check if ANY player would deviate
    • A cell is NE if no player benefits from unilateral change

Reinforcement Learning

  1. Value iteration:

    • Don’t forget the reward r(s)
    • Multiply by γ AFTER computing expected value
    • Take MAX over actions

  2. Discount factor:

    • Lower γ = care more about present
    • Higher γ = care more about future

Neural Networks

  1. Leaky ReLU:

    • For negative inputs: output = α×input
    • LeakyReLU(−0.5) with α=0.2 gives −0.1

  2. ReLU gradient:

    • 1 for positive inputs
    • 0 for negative inputs (NOT everywhere!)

Laboratory Assignment 11: Identifying a Mystery Fossil

Overview

Choose one of the mystery fossils designated by a different color:

  • RED
  • ORANGE
  • YELLOW
  • GREEN
  • VIOLET

You may choose any one of these colors. You should find the virtual lab component with your mystery fossil and open it on Canvas. The virtual lab presents the mystery fossil together with a modern human cranium and the Sts 5 specimen of Australopithecus africanus. These two specimens are there to help you assess the size and shape of your mystery fossil in comparison to other virtual labs.

Offline copies of the virtual labs

The interactive 3D viewers downloaded from Canvas are kept in this course’s assets/. Open them in a browser: GREEN · ORANGE · RED · VIOLET · YELLOW

You will need to assess the features of your mystery fossil and how those features compare to five species or extinct populations of hominins, as described in the rubric below. Your task is to assign the mystery fossil to a species. The mystery fossil will be broken or fragmented, and it may not preserve all the features that you might like to compare with one or another of the species.

Questions

1. What is the color of your mystery fossil?

Orange

2. Assessment of the condition of the fossil (2 pts)

This part of your written assignment should describe the parts of the cranium that are preserved in your mystery fossil, and the parts that are missing. You should also note any clear evidence of distortion of the fossil that affects its shape, such as flattening or fragmentation.

Full Credit Requirements

  • Identify the main cranial bones that are present and absent
  • Note whether distortion is present
  • Provide detailed descriptions for the entire cranium and each specific bone
  • Do not just list all the bones

It has the frontal bone and upper face, including the eye sockets and part of the upper jaw.

The entire back and base of the skull which are most of the parietals, occipital, temporals, zygomatic arches, and the mandible are missing/

The skull is somewhat distorted, with asymmetrical, irregularly shaped orbits and a lumpy surface that suggest post-mortem damage and erosion. The right eye socket seems noticable deeper compared to the left, which maybe could be damage or injury.

3. Comparisons of your mystery fossil to known species

For each of these five species or populations, you should find 5 features that you can compare with your mystery fossil.

Important

Only use traits discussed in lab section. Do not make up your own or use other traits from the internet!

Full credit on this portion will include 5 sentences for each feature within each comparison, making clear the anatomy of the mystery fossil and the comparative species. Each should end with a statement of the number of shared and different features that you identify. Full credit is not just a list with single-word descriptions; the section should describe the features in a way that a reader can understand what was compared. Full credit will provide a count of the shared and different features for each species.

Full Credit Example

These are not real hominin traits, just an example of the format:

  1. The mystery fossil has purple fur, a trait not found in Australopithecus.
  2. The mystery fossil has wings, unlike Australopithecus.
  3. The mystery fossil has 3 fingers, which is a trait shared by Australopithecus.
  4. The mystery fossil has one eye, unlike Australopithecus.
  5. Australopithecus has round ears, which is different from the mystery fossil.

Out of the features I compared, this skull is different from Australopithecus in 4 out of the 5 features and similar in 1.

Comparison Guidelines

  • Comparisons should only be made using traits that are either on your mystery fossil or in the species you are comparing it to
  • For example, if your mystery fossil does not have a sagittal crest, you cannot use absence of a sagittal crest as a similarity in any non-Paranthropus comparison
  • You may not use a trait that is no longer preserved in your mystery fossil (e.g., if the fossil does not have teeth, you may never use teeth size as a valid feature to compare)

3a. Compare the mystery fossil to Australopithecus (3 pts)

  • The mystery fossil and Australopithecus share similar degrees of prognathism, as both have a moderately projecting lower face instead of a flat one.
  • Both the mystery fossil and Australopithecus have smaller brain sizes than modern humans, but the mystery fossil’s cranial vault looks slightly higher, suggesting a somewhat larger brain.
  • The skull of Australopithecus shows strong postorbital constriction, and the mystery fossil also narrows behind the eye sockets, although the constriction seems a bit less extreme.
  • Australopithecus generally has only modest brow ridges, while the mystery fossil has a thicker, more continuous supraorbital torus, so the brow region is more pronounced in the mystery fossil.
  • Both Australopithecus and the mystery fossil have sloping foreheads, where the frontal bone angles back instead of rising vertically like in modern humans.
  • They are similar in 3 of the 5 traits and different in 2.

3b. Compare the mystery fossil to Paranthropus (3 pts)

  • Both Paranthropus and the mystery fossil show clear postorbital constriction, with the skulls narrowing behind the orbits rather than staying wide and rounded.
  • Paranthropus has a very strongly projecting, robust face, while the mystery fossil has only moderate prognathism, so the mystery fossil is less projecting.
  • The brain size of Paranthropus is relatively small compared to later Homo, but the mystery fossil’s cranial vault looks somewhat larger and higher, suggesting a larger brain.
  • The supraorbital torus in Paranthropus is present but not as continuous and thick as in classic Homo erectus, whereas the mystery fossil shows a more pronounced brow ridge that looks more like early Homo than like Paranthropus.
  • Both Paranthropus and the mystery fossil have sloping foreheads, with the frontal bone angling backward instead of forming a tall vertical forehead.
  • They are similar in 3 of the 5 traits and different in 2.

3c. Compare the mystery fossil to Homo habilis (3 pts)

  • The mystery fossil and Homo habilis both have moderate prognathism, with faces that project somewhat forward but are less projecting than those of Australopithecus.
  • Both Homo habilis and the mystery fossil show postorbital constriction, as the skulls narrow behind the orbits instead of staying broad.
  • The forehead in both Homo habilis and the mystery fossil slopes back from the brow region, rather than rising straight up like in modern humans.
  • Homo habilis typically has brow ridges that are noticeable but not as thick and continuous as in Homo erectus, while the mystery fossil’s supraorbital torus appears more robust.
  • The brain size of Homo habilis is larger than in Australopithecus, and the mystery fossil’s cranial vault may be slightly larger still, suggesting a somewhat bigger brain than typical Homo habilis.
  • They are similar in 3 of the 5 traits and different in 2.

3d. Compare the mystery fossil to Homo erectus (3 pts)

  • The mystery fossil and Homo erectus both have moderate prognathism, with faces that project somewhat but are less projecting than those of Australopithecus or Paranthropus.
  • Both the mystery fossil and Homo erectus show a strong supraorbital torus, with thick brow ridges above the eye sockets that are more pronounced than in Homo habilis or modern humans.
  • The forehead of Homo erectus slopes back noticeably from the brow region, and the mystery fossil shows the same kind of sloping frontal bone.
  • In both Homo erectus and the mystery fossil, the cranium narrows behind the orbits, indicating postorbital constriction rather than a very broad, rounded vault.
  • The nasal cavity of Homo erectus is relatively large compared to earlier hominins, and the mystery fossil also has a fairly large nasal opening, suggesting a similar nasal cavity size.
  • They are similar in all 5 of the traits.

3e. Compare the mystery fossil to Neandertals (3 pts)

  • Neandertals have very large brains and big, rounded cranial vaults, while the mystery fossil’s preserved vault looks smaller and less expanded.
  • Both Neandertals and the mystery fossil have strong brow ridges, with a clear supraorbital torus above the orbits.
  • The forehead of Neandertals slopes back more than in modern humans, and the mystery fossil also has a sloping forehead.
  • Neandertals have relatively little postorbital constriction because of their large brains and wide parietals, while the mystery fossil narrows more behind the orbits.
  • Both Neandertals and the mystery fossil have relatively large nasal cavities compared to the rest of the face, rather than a small, narrow nasal opening.
  • They are similar in 3 of the 5 traits and different in 2.

4. Assessment of the best match for the mystery fossil (2 pts)

Provide your best guess about the identity of your mystery fossil. Your assessment should note the features that are the most persuasive or informative in your perspective. You may give one or two likely possibilities and discuss why they may be hard to distinguish from each other.

I think the mystery fossil is probably Homo erectus, because it has a sloping forehead, a pronounced brow ridge, and a relatively large nasal opening.

You should also discuss what other species that were not in question 3 that you learned about in lecture or lab, and why this skull may or may not belong to those species. Additionally, what other information would be helpful to know about this fossil that may aid in your assessment of its species?

Chapter 6: Primate Mating Systems

Overview

  • Every primate behavior ultimately exists because it contributed to reproduction in ancestral populations, so a species’ mating system—how animals find mates and care for young—is central to understanding primate societies.
  • Primate reproduction is shaped by a shared mammalian heritage: females gestate internally and lactate, which commits them to heavy investment in each offspring; males’ contribution is far more variable.
  • Unequal parental investment evolves when one sex (usually the male) can profitably trade parenting effort for extra matings; because only females lactate, when just one sex invests it is invariably the female.
  • Female reproductive success is limited mainly by access to resources, and varies with age, longevity, dominance rank, and the strength of social bonds.
  • Because males can sire many offspring, they compete for mates; sexual selection (especially intrasexual, male–male competition) drives traits like large body size, big canines, and—where females mate with many males—large testes.
  • Male tactics range from paternal investment in pair-bonded species to fierce competition over group residence and rank in non–pair-bonded species; infanticide is an adaptive male strategy under specific conditions, and females have evolved counterstrategies.

Chapter objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • Explain why reproduction is the central act of every living thing.
  • Describe how mammalian reproductive biology shapes the reproductive strategies of female primates.
  • Discuss the factors that drive variation in female reproductive success.
  • Describe sexual selection and explain why it can favor traits that ordinary natural selection would not.
  • Explain how competition among males over access to females shapes male reproductive strategies.
  • Explain why infanticide can be an adaptive strategy for male primates under certain conditions.

The Language of Adaptive Explanations

In evolutionary biology, strategy does not imply a conscious plan (as in a general’s tactics). It refers to a set of behaviors that occur in a particular functional context—foraging, mating, parenting—produced by natural selection acting on the motivations, preferences, and capacities that govern behavior. Strategies that raised reproductive success in ancestral populations are adaptations.

Likewise, cost and benefit describe how a behavior affects genetic fitness: beneficial behaviors raise fitness, costly ones lower it. Ultimately both should be measured as changes in reproductive success, but because that is hard to track in long-lived animals, researchers often use indirect proxies (such as foraging efficiency) and assume that, all else equal, gains in efficiency translate into gains in fitness.

The Evolution of Reproductive Strategies

Parental care varies enormously across the animal kingdom—from frogs that abandon their eggs to birds and mammals that shelter, feed, and protect their young. Among primates, mothers always nurse and frequently provide extensive care, whereas fathers’ behavior is highly variable: in many species males give offspring nothing beyond sperm, while in a minority they are devoted parents.

The amount and balance of investment by each sex has profound consequences for social behavior and morphology, because the selection pressures on the sexes differ sharply depending on whether investment is shared or lopsided.

Why males often don’t invest. Although helping would seem to raise offspring survival, time, energy, and resources are finite, so parenting effort trades off against mating effort. Even where most males help, a few have a heritable tendency to invest less; their offspring get less care (lowering survival) but they gain extra matings. The tendency to invest less spreads when the fitness gained from additional matings outweighs the fitness lost to reduced offspring care. Thus unequal investment is favored when (1) additional mates are easy to acquire, or (2) offspring raised by one parent still do well, so extra parental help adds little.

Why the investing sex is the female. Nothing in this logic by itself says the investing sex must be female—indeed, in sea horses and some fish and birds (rheas, spotted sandpipers, jacanas), males do the parenting. But in mammals, pregnancy and especially lactation commit females: offspring depend on the mother for nourishment, so she cannot abandon them without crippling their survival, and males cannot rear young alone. Hence when only one sex invests, it is always the female. (Selection has not produced lactating males because the developmental changes required would likely make them sterile—a developmental constraint.)

Reproductive Strategies of Females

Pregnancy and lactation are costly and time-consuming for all female primates. Gestation ranges from about 59 days (mouse lemur) to 255 days (gorilla); larger species have longer pregnancies (Figure 6.5), but primates gestate longer than body size alone would predict because their large brains develop slowly. With a long period of post-birth dependence, mothers must support both themselves and growing infants (which may reach ~30% of maternal weight by weaning).

Figure 6.5. Across primates, as in other mammals, maternal body size is correlated with gestation length. Great apes have the longest pregnancies, while small-bodied strepsirrhines have relatively short ones.

Because each infant is so expensive, a female produces only a small number of surviving young in a lifetime—a baboon first reproducing at 6–7 years and living to 30 might bear about a dozen, of which many die young. Each infant therefore represents a large share of a female’s lifetime fitness, so mothers are strongly committed to each one.

Resources limit female reproduction. Females need a minimum nutritional level to ovulate and conceive, and reproductive success is limited by food availability. When food improves, females grow faster, mature earlier, and shorten interbirth intervals. Provisioning experiments in Japan, where wild macaques were fed supplementary foods, produced rapid group growth—direct evidence that resource availability caps population growth.

Sources of Variation in Female Reproductive Performance

Age. Age-specific fertility rates show that young (primiparous) females reproduce less successfully than middle-aged ones. First-time mountain gorilla mothers, for example, have ~50% higher infant mortality and ~20% longer interbirth intervals than older females. Young females are still growing, so energy goes to their own development as well as the infant, and they may lack mothering experience. Unlike humans, most primate females keep reproducing throughout life: the age of last birth is close to the age at death (Figure 6.10 in the text). The postreproductive period is only ~1–6% of the lifespan in these species, versus ~43% in !Kung human foragers.

Longevity. “Showing up” matters: the longer a female lives, the more offspring she rears. Longevity accounts for roughly 50–70% of the variance in lifetime reproductive success among female baboons that reach maturity, dwarfing other sources—though why some females live longer remains poorly understood.

Dominance rank. Where females form dominance hierarchies (see A Closer Look 6.1), high rank confers priority of access to the best food. In one baboon study, high-ranking females ate ~30% more per day than low-ranking ones, though disparities vary because low-rankers may compensate by feeding (more dangerously) on the group’s edge. Rank correlates with reproductive performance in many species: offspring of high-ranking baboons grow faster and mature earlier; high-ranking vervets and gorillas have shorter interbirth intervals; high-ranking chimpanzee offspring are more likely to survive to weaning. In gray langurs, rank declines with age, so young high-ranking females outreproduce older low-ranking ones. In cooperatively breeding marmosets and tamarins, usually only the dominant female breeds; subordinates often fail to cycle, and the dominant female may kill subordinates’ infants to reduce competition.

Social bonds. Females invest time in grooming and associating with others even when foraging is hard, suggesting bonds matter. Females who lose close companions to predators show rising cortisol (a stress marker). Long-term baboon data show that more socially integrated females rear more surviving infants, independent of rank—and sociality can offset the costs of low rank. The mechanism is unclear: possibilities include better predator protection or stress reduction benefiting health.

Reproductive Trade-offs

Because effort is finite, a mother cannot maximize both the quality and the quantity of her offspring; investing heavily in one infant means less for others. Maternal behavior tracks this trade-off as the infant grows. Newborns ride in constant contact and are retrieved when they stray; as infants become competent—exploring, sampling foods, heeding alarm calls—mothers actively encourage independence, resisting suckling attempts and limiting nursing to brief bouts. Carrying and feeding heavier older infants is costly, but because those infants can increasingly fend for themselves, mothers can safely scale back investment and reallocate it to future young. Since lactation suppresses ovulation in many species, a female must wean one infant before conceiving the next.

Sexual Selection and Male Mating Strategies

Because females invest heavily and are limited by food rather than mates, while males can potentially father many offspring, males compete for access to females. Traits that improve success in this competition spread through sexual selection—a special category of natural selection that favors traits raising mating success and is strongest in whichever sex has the more limited access to mates. Such traits (the peacock’s train, red deer antlers, the hamadryas mane) can spread even if they reduce survival, an outcome ordinary natural selection would not favor.

Sexual selection is often stronger than ordinary natural selection because male reproductive success varies far more than female success. Long-term lion data show the most successful males far outreproduce the most successful females; many males sire nothing while a few sire many. Greater variance means stronger selection, so sexual selection on males can exceed natural selection on females. (In sea horses, where males invest and females do not, the pattern reverses and sexual selection acts more strongly on females.)

Sexual selection has two forms: intrasexual selection (competition among males) and intersexual selection (female choice). Because there is little evidence that female choice plays a major role in primates, the chapter focuses on intrasexual selection.

Intrasexual Selection

In its simplest form, males drive rivals away from females; consistent winners reproduce more. This favors large body size, large canines, and other weaponry. Where the sexes consistently differ in size or appearance, they are sexually dimorphic. Body size reflects competing pressures—large males fight better and resist predators but need more food and mature later. Because the fitness payoff to a very successful male exceeds that to a very successful female, intrasexual competition among males is quantitatively greater than competition among females, and it drives the evolution of sexual dimorphism.

The clearest test uses group composition. Male competition should be most intense where males are most outnumbered by females—seemingly paradoxical, but because the sex ratio at birth is roughly even, one-male groups generate many surplus “bachelor males” pressing on resident males, whereas in pair-bonded species each male has one female. Comparative analyses (Harvey and Clutton-Brock) confirm that dimorphism tracks group type: little dimorphism in pair-bonded species (gibbons, titis, marmosets), the most in one-male, multifemale species (gorillas, black-and-white colobus), and intermediate dimorphism in multimale, multifemale species (Figure 6.23).

Figure 6.23. The degree of sexual dimorphism tracks the ratio of males to females in social groups. Both (a) relative canine size and (b) body-size dimorphism are greatest in species that form one-male, multifemale groups and least in pair-bonded species, with multimale, multifemale species in between.

Sperm competition. In multimale, multifemale groups, a female in estrus—the receptive, fertile phase—may mate with several males in one cycle, so sexual selection favors greater sperm production: the male depositing the most sperm has the best chance of fertilization. Sperm competition matters little in pair-bonded species (females mate mainly with their partner, so mate guarding pays more than large sperm output) or in one-male groups (competition is over group access, favoring fighting ability). As predicted, relative testis size is much larger in multimale, multifemale species than in pair-bonded or one-male species (Figure 6.24).

Figure 6.24. Relative testis size (observed testis weight divided by the weight expected for body size) is much larger in multimale, multifemale species than in pair-bonded or one-male, multifemale species, matching the prediction that sperm competition is most intense where females mate with multiple males.

Male Reproductive Tactics

Morphology suggests male–male competition is weaker in pair-bonded than in non–pair-bonded species. Sexual selection shapes male tactics as well as male anatomy.

Investing Males

In pair-bonded species, males don’t compete directly over females; their success depends on holding a territory, finding a mate, and rearing surviving young, so mate guarding and paternal care are key tactics. Genetic studies show pair bonds are not strictly monogamous—about 10% of white-handed gibbon offspring come from extrapair matings—which gives males reason to stay close to and monitor their partners. Male gibbons largely take responsibility for staying near their mates and groom them more than they are groomed in return. Pair-bonded males often invest heavily: male titi monkeys, owl monkeys, and siamangs carry, groom, share food with, and protect infants.

In cooperatively breeding species (marmosets and tamarins), groups typically contain a dominant pair plus helpers of both sexes, and the dominant male usually monopolizes matings. These species often bear twins at short intervals, and male help is real but costly—males lose weight while carrying infants. Garber’s data show groups with more adult males rear more surviving infants, whereas extra females do not boost infant survival, indicating male helpers raise female fertility even though the reproductive payoff to individual helper males is uncertain.

Male–Male Competition in Groups without Pair Bonds

In non–pair-bonded (polygynous and polygynandrous) species, male success hinges on gaining access to groups of unrelated females and to receptive females within them, generating intense competition and large disparities among males.

  • One-male groups. Resident males face constant pressure from outsiders. Gelada males endure multiday takeover battles; gray langur males form all-male bands that oust residents and then compete among themselves, so male tenure is often short. Residence does not guarantee exclusivity—in patas and blue monkeys, outside males slip in to mate during the breeding season. Some species switch flexibly: red howler males form one-male groups in sparse forests but pair up to defend larger female groups where competition is fierce. In geladas, about a third of units include a “follower” male alongside the leader; followers help repel bachelor bands and extend the leader’s tenure, and although leaders sire ~83% of infants, followers gain limited reproductive success.
  • Multimale groups. Here competition centers on access to receptive females more than on group membership, though joining a new group is still difficult. Competition is usually mediated through dominance relationships set in contests ranging from threats to escalated fights; rank tracks physical condition, with prime-age males usually dominant.

Genetic paternity testing has strengthened the link between male rank and reproductive success. High-ranking baboons sire disproportionately many offspring (Figure 6.32 in the text) and preferentially mate-guard females during conceptive cycles; the top Taï Forest chimpanzee sires nearly half of all infants; top white-faced capuchins sire 38–70% across groups. Rank is not the only factor—a top male monopolizes most effectively when few other males and few simultaneously cycling females are present. Males typically disperse before their daughters mature, and inbreeding is largely avoided: in capuchins, alpha males sired 79% of unrelated females’ offspring but only 6% of their own daughters’.

Figure 6.31. In baboons, male dominance rank is tightly linked to age and physical condition: males peak in rank around age 8 and decline thereafter, and male reproductive success closely follows male age and rank.

Infanticide

Sarah Blaffer Hrdy first recognized that intense male competition could favor infanticide as a male reproductive tactic. The logic: a nursing female does not resume cycling for a long time, but if her infant dies, lactation stops and she becomes receptive much sooner. A male who takes over a group or rises to the top can therefore benefit by killing unweaned infants he did not sire. This sexual selection infanticide hypothesis was initially controversial—there were no direct observations and many doubted such violence could be an evolved strategy—but infanticide by males is now documented in roughly 40 primate species (and many non-primates, such as lions), with 60+ witnessed attacks in the wild.

The hypothesis yields four predictions, all supported: infanticide should (1) accompany changes in male residence or rank; (2) target unweaned infants whose deaths hasten the mother’s return to cycling; (3) spare the killer’s own infants; and (4) yield reproductive benefits to the killer. Van Schaik’s compilation of 55 witnessed cases found that ~85% followed changes in male residence or rank, most victims were unweaned, only 7% were committed by males who could have sired the infant, and in 45–70% of cases the male later mated with the victim’s mother. Infanticide is a substantial source of mortality—about a third of infant deaths in several gorilla, baboon, langur, and howler populations, and ~40% of gelada infants killed after takeovers.

Female counterstrategies. Because infanticide is disastrous for mothers, females have evolved responses. Direct defense rarely works given male size advantages. Instead, females confuse paternity—since males kill mainly when paternity is unambiguous. Gray langur females are receptive for about nine days and can ovulate anytime within it, solicit and mate with multiple males throughout (not concentrated near ovulation), and even solicit males after takeovers when already pregnant—all obscuring the timing of conception (Figure 6.34 in the text). Gelada females take a different route, terminating pregnancies in the days after a takeover; though seemingly costly, this can pay off because such females have shorter interbirth intervals than those who carry to term only to lose the infant—an adaptive, evolved response, not a conscious decision. In baboons, new mothers form close “friendships” with one or two males who defend and carry their infants; female cortisol spikes when immigrant males arrive but is buffered by having a male associate, and males’ protective responses to a female’s distress cease if her infant dies—evidence these bonds guard against infanticide.

Why still controversial? The data fit Hrdy’s hypothesis well, yet some resist it. Volker Sommer argues the resistance reflects the naturalistic fallacy—assuming that what occurs in nature is therefore right or justified—and a fear that accepting infanticide as adaptive would excuse it in humans. But drawing moral lessons from animal behavior is misguided: human morality rests on culturally evolved norms, which is precisely why the naturalistic fallacy is faulty reasoning.

A Closer Look 6.1: Dominance Hierarchies

Across many species (crickets, chickens, chimpanzees), one-on-one contests have predictable outcomes when individuals differ reliably in size, strength, experience, or aggressiveness. When the outcomes between two animals are consistent, a dominance relationship exists, and individuals can be assigned ranks. For four hypothetical females—Blue, Turquoise, Green, Purple—where each beats all those below it and loses to all above, the relationships are transitive, and when every trio is transitive the whole hierarchy is linear. Such data are summarized in a dominance matrix, with winners down the side and losers across the top and cell values counting wins; because lower-ranked females never defeat higher-ranked ones, the cells below the diagonal stay empty. Rank can have real fitness consequences: in long-tailed macaques, both group size and rank shape lifetime reproductive success, with high-ranking females outreproducing low-ranking ones in groups of any size.

Key terms

  • strategy
  • primiparous
  • multiparous
  • dominance
  • dominance matrix
  • transitive
  • sexual selection
  • intrasexual selection
  • intersexual selection
  • bachelor males
  • estrus
  • sexual selection infanticide hypothesis

Study questions

  1. Why is reproductive success central to evolution by natural selection, and what “currency” do biologists mean by cost and benefit?
  2. How do polygyny and polyandry differ? Why might males and females prefer different mating systems, and why is polygyny more common than polyandry?
  3. Some researchers argue reproductive seasonality evolved as a way for females to manipulate their reproductive options. How would seasonality change females’ options, and why might it be advantageous?
  4. What would you infer about social organization in (a) a species with equal-sized sexes but relatively large male testes, and (b) a species where males are much larger than females but have small testes? Why do these relationships hold?
  5. Why is male fitness typically more variable than female fitness in mammals, and what does this imply for selection on each sex?
  6. What factors shape female reproductive success, and how do they generate variance in it?
  7. What aspects of the selective forces on parental care does the term “investment” capture?
  8. Lay out the logic of the sexual selection infanticide hypothesis, list its predictions, and explain why each follows.
  9. Why might infanticide be more common in one-male groups than in multimale or pair-bonded species?

Chapter 27: Interlude: Thread API

Overview

  • The POSIX (pthreads) library exposes a small core API: create/join threads, lock/unlock mutexes, and wait/signal on condition variables.
  • pthread_create() spawns a thread running a given function; pthread_join() blocks until a specified thread finishes and optionally collects its return value.
  • Arguments and return values are passed as void *, letting you pass anything — but never return a pointer to a variable on the thread’s stack, which vanishes when the thread returns.
  • Mutexes provide mutual exclusion; they must be initialized (statically or via pthread_mutex_init) and their return codes checked. Wrapper functions that assert success keep code clean.
  • Condition variables let a thread sleep until another signals it. pthread_cond_wait() must be called with the associated lock held; it atomically releases the lock and sleeps, then re-acquires before returning.
  • Two enduring rules: always recheck the condition in a while loop (not if), and never hand-roll signaling with a spinning flag — use condition variables.

The crux

What interface should the OS/thread library offer to create and control threads, so it is both easy to use and useful? This chapter is best treated as a reference; later chapters develop locks and condition variables slowly with many examples.

27.1 Thread Creation

Creating a thread takes four arguments:

  • thread — pointer to a pthread_t the call initializes; you use it later to refer to this thread.
  • attr — optional attributes (stack size, priority); pass NULL for defaults.
  • start_routine — a function pointer: the function the new thread begins running. It takes one void * and returns a void *.
  • arg — the single argument handed to start_routine.

The void * types are the trick that lets you pass (and return) any type. To pass several values, package them in a struct and pass its address:

27.2 Thread Completion

To wait for a thread to finish, use:

The first argument names which thread to wait for; the second is a pointer to where the thread’s return value should be stored (pass NULL if you don’t care). A thread can return a value by, e.g., malloc-ing a struct and returning its pointer, which join then hands back.

Never return a pointer to the thread's stack

When the thread returns, its stack-allocated r is gone; the returned pointer dangles. Return heap-allocated data (or a value that fits in the pointer) instead.

Not all multi-threaded code uses join. A web server might spin up worker threads that live forever, with the main thread feeding them requests indefinitely. But a parallel computation that splits work into threads typically joins them to ensure all work completes before moving on.

The pthreads basics — creation/join, mutexes, and condition variables — are nearly all you need to write robust, efficient multi-threaded code. The API is the easy part; the hard part is the logic of building correct concurrent programs.

Thread-programming guidelines

  • Keep it simple — tricky thread interactions breed bugs.
  • Minimize interactions between threads, and use tried-and-true patterns.
  • Initialize all locks and condition variables.
  • Check return codes on every call.
  • Be careful passing/returning data — never share a pointer to a stack variable.
  • Remember each thread has its own stack — share data via the heap or globals.
  • Always use condition variables to signal, never a bare flag.
  • Read the man pages (man -k pthread).

Key terms

  • pthreads — the POSIX threads library/standard.
  • pthread_create / pthread_join — spawn a thread / wait for one to finish.
  • function pointer — a pointer to the routine a new thread will run.
  • mutex — POSIX name for a lock providing mutual exclusion.
  • PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER / pthread_mutex_init — static / dynamic lock initialization.
  • wrapper — a thin function (e.g., Pthread_mutex_lock) that calls the real routine and asserts success.
  • trylock / timedlock — non-blocking / time-bounded lock acquisition.
  • condition variable — a queue threads wait on until signaled.
  • pthread_cond_wait / pthread_cond_signal — sleep on / wake one waiter of a CV.
  • spurious wakeup — waking from wait without a corresponding signal; why you must recheck.
  • coarse- vs. fine-grained locking — one big lock vs. many small locks for more concurrency.

Lecture 25: Spark MLlib

Overview

This lecture introduces Spark MLlib, Spark’s machine learning library for distributed model training and prediction. We cover the fundamentals of supervised learning, compare the training and prediction APIs across scikit-learn, PyTorch, and Spark MLlib, and then dive deep into decision trees — how they make predictions, how they are trained, and how the PLANET algorithm enables efficient distributed training on large datasets.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

  • Perform common machine learning tasks (train/test split, preprocessing, pipelining, training, prediction, and evaluation) using Spark MLlib
  • Describe how decision trees make predictions
  • Describe how the PLANET (Parallel Learner for Assembling Numerous Ensemble Trees) algorithm efficiently trains decision trees on large, distributed data

Machine Learning Overview

Machine learning (ML) is a broad field with three classic categories:

  • Reinforcement learning: An agent makes a series of actions to maximize a reward signal
  • Unsupervised learning: The algorithm looks for general patterns in data without labeled outputs
  • Supervised learning: Train models to predict outputs given inputs — this is the focus of this lecture and Spark MLlib

Models and Predictions

In supervised learning, a model is essentially a function that returns predictions. The model takes some input information and produces a prediction:

The type of prediction determines the task:

  • Regression: The prediction is numeric (e.g., 1, 2, 3) — predicting a continuous value
  • Classification: The prediction is categorical (e.g., A, B, C) — predicting a discrete class label

For example, a weather forecasting model takes today’s and yesterday’s temperatures as inputs and returns tomorrow’s predicted temperature:

The computation inside a model usually involves calculations (multiply, add) with various numbers called parameters. Training is the process of finding parameter values that result in good predictions for known training data.

Learning from Data

In a supervised learning dataset, columns are divided into feature columns (the inputs, often called X) and a label column (the output to predict, often called y). Given a table with features x1, x2 and label y, some rows have known labels while others have unknown labels that we want to predict.

The key question is: how can the rows where we DO know y help us predict the rows where we do not?

Train/Validation/Test Split

The data is randomly split into three subsets:

  1. Training set: Used to fit/train model parameters
  2. Validation set: Used to compare models and select the best one
  3. Test set: Used to evaluate the final chosen model on unseen data

The workflow proceeds as follows:

The validation set is used to pick which model generalizes better. The test set then gives an unbiased estimate of how well the chosen model will perform on truly unseen data.

Warning

A model that performs well on training data but poorly on validation or test data has overfitted — it memorized the training examples rather than learning general patterns. The winning model on the validation set might also perform slightly worse on the test set because the model selection process itself introduces a subtle bias toward the validation data.

Training and Predicting APIs

Three popular ML frameworks each have slightly different APIs for training and prediction. Understanding these differences is important when transitioning between single-machine and distributed ML.

Training

scikit-learn — models are mutable; fitting modifies the object in place:

PyTorch — models are also mutable; training uses an explicit loop with an optimizer and loss function:

Spark MLlib — models are immutable; fitting returns a new model object:

Note

The key difference is that in Spark MLlib, calling .fit() returns a new fitted model object rather than modifying the original. This immutable design aligns with Spark’s functional programming philosophy and its use of immutable DataFrames (see lecture-16).

Data Representation

In scikit-learn and PyTorch, features (X) and labels (y) are typically separate arrays or tensors. The model takes X as input and returns y as output.

In Spark MLlib, features and labels are columns in a DataFrame. The transform method takes a DataFrame with feature columns and returns a new DataFrame with the original columns plus a prediction column appended.

Features Column

Spark MLlib expects a single features column that contains vectors. Each vector typically combines values from multiple individual columns. For example, if you have columns with values 2 and 3, the features column would contain the vector (2, 3). This consolidation is done using a VectorAssembler transformer during preprocessing.

Spark MLlib Terminology

Spark and scikit-learn use many of the same terms but with very different meanings. Understanding this terminology is critical for using Spark MLlib correctly.

Transformer

In scikit-learn: An object with a .transform method that takes a DataFrame and returns a different DataFrame. Used as a preprocessing step for a model.

In Spark MLlib: An object with a .transform method that takes a DataFrame and returns the original DataFrame with one or more additional columns. A fitted model is itself a transformer — it adds a prediction column.

Estimator

In scikit-learn: An object with .fit and .predict methods. Calling .fit modifies the object. Makes predictions after learning parameters.

In Spark MLlib: An object with a .fit method that returns a new object (a transformer). An unfitted model is an estimator; calling .fit on it returns a fitted model (a transformer).

Tip

In Spark MLlib, think of it this way: Estimator + Data = Transformer. The estimator learns from data and produces a transformer that can add predictions to new DataFrames.

Pipelines

Both scikit-learn and Spark support pipelines — a series of stages (transformers and estimators) where .fit/.transform are called as appropriate on each stage.

In Spark, a Pipeline is itself an estimator. When you call .fit() on a Pipeline:

  1. For each transformer stage: call .transform on the data, passing the result to the next stage
  2. For each estimator stage: call .fit to produce a transformer
  3. The result is a PipelineModel containing all transformers (including the fitted estimator, now a transformer)

When you call .transform() on the resulting PipelineModel, it sequentially calls .transform on each stage, passing the data through the entire pipeline to produce final predictions.

Spark MLlib Packages

There are two Spark MLlib packages:

  • pyspark.mllib — the older API based on RDDs (deprecated)
  • pyspark.ml — the newer API based on DataFrames (preferred)

Always use pyspark.ml for new code, as it integrates with Spark’s DataFrame API and benefits from the Catalyst optimizer.

Decision Trees

Decision trees are a widely used ML model that can handle both classification and regression tasks. They are conceptually similar to nested if/else statements, where each internal node tests a condition on a feature and each leaf node provides a prediction.

Structure and Predictions

A decision tree consists of:

  • A root node at the top, which asks the first question about the data
  • Decision nodes (internal nodes) that split data based on a feature condition
  • Leaf nodes at the bottom, which hold the prediction

For example, a decision tree for deciding whether to accept a job offer might look like:

Features and labels can be either numeric or categorical. Decision trees handle both naturally.

Info

If a decision tree is very large, many subtrees might be similar. This redundancy motivates ensemble methods that combine many smaller trees instead of one large tree.

Ensemble Methods

An ensemble combines many simple models that vote together. Many simple decision trees (each trained on a subset of rows or columns) together are often better than one large tree. Common ensemble approaches include:

  • Random forest: Train many trees independently on random subsets of data, then use majority voting (classification) or averaging (regression)
  • Gradient-boosted trees: Train trees sequentially, with each new tree correcting errors from the previous ones

A Spark cluster can train many trees in a random forest simultaneously, making it a natural fit for distributed computing.

Tree Methods vs. Deep Learning

Tree-based methods remain highly relevant even in the age of deep learning. Deep learning excels at unstructured data (images, text, audio) where it performs implicit feature extraction. However, for structured/tabular data (tables with well-defined columns), conventional machine learning methods like decision trees and gradient-boosted trees are often competitive or even superior to deep learning approaches.

Training Decision Trees

Evaluating Tree Quality: Impurity

To determine whether a decision tree is good, we measure the impurity of its leaf nodes. Impurity quantifies how non-uniform the label values (y) are within each leaf.

Consider a dataset with features x1, x2 and label y:

A tree that splits on x1 > 2.5 produces leaves with high variance in y values (5 and 8.6 in one leaf, 8.8 and 5.2 in the other). A tree that splits on x2 > 0 produces leaves with low variance (5 and 5.2 together, 8.6 and 8.8 together). The second tree is better because its leaves group similar y values together.

When a new data point arrives, it falls into a leaf, and we predict the average (regression) or majority class (classification) of the training examples in that leaf. Low impurity means the training examples in each leaf are similar, so the prediction is more reliable.

Splitting Nodes

Training a decision tree works by recursively splitting nodes:

  1. Start with one node containing all the data
  2. Find the best split point (which feature and which threshold) that creates two children with the lowest impurity
  3. Recursively split the child nodes
  4. Eventually stop splitting

For a node with data, the algorithm considers every possible split:

  • For each feature column, sort the data by that column
  • Walk through the sorted values, considering each gap between consecutive values as a potential split point
  • Compute impurity for each candidate split incrementally (by updating counts as you move one row at a time)
  • Choose the split that reduces impurity the most across all features and thresholds

Tip

By sorting each feature column and then scanning incrementally, impurity can be computed for each split point by looking at just one additional row of data. There is no need to loop over all rows for every possible split point.

When to Stop Splitting

Overfitting occurs when a tree is too complex — it memorizes the training data rather than learning general patterns. A simpler tree might predict a 50% probability for a category at a given node, while a more complex tree might overfit and predict 100% for a node that only had one training example.

Several approaches control tree complexity:

  • Set a maximum tree height (depth limit)
  • Set a minimum number of rows required in a node before it can be split
  • Prune the tree after training to remove unhelpful or excessive splits

The PLANET Algorithm

When the dataset is too large to fit on a single machine, the in-memory training approach breaks down. The data is partitioned across many Spark workers, and sorting each column would require expensive network shuffles. Furthermore, if you loop over every possible split point sequentially, only one worker computes at a time — this is not parallel.

The PLANET (Parallel Learner for Assembling Numerous Ensemble Trees) algorithm solves this problem. Originally implemented as MapReduce jobs by researchers at Google, it is used by Spark’s DecisionTreeRegressor and DecisionTreeClassifier.

Hybrid Approach

PLANET uses a hybrid strategy:

  • In-memory splitting for nodes with few enough rows to fit in one worker’s memory
  • Distributed splitting (with fewer, pre-defined split points) for nodes with too much data

Step 1: Compute Equi-Depth Histograms

Before training begins, PLANET computes an equi-depth histogram for every feature column. Each bucket in the histogram contains approximately the same number of samples. The bucket boundaries become the candidate split points for the distributed algorithm.

The maxBins parameter controls how many bins (buckets) are created per feature. This limits the number of candidate split points, making the distributed algorithm tractable.

Warning

The number of bins must be greater than the largest number of unique values in any categorical column. If maxBins is too small, Spark will raise an error.

Step 2: Split Points — In-Memory vs. Distributed

The in-memory algorithm considers split points based on every unique value in the sorted data — one split between each pair of consecutive values. The distributed algorithm uses the histogram bucket boundaries as split points instead. Because there are only a small number of pre-defined split points, every Spark task knows the split info for every column, enabling executors to collaborate with minimal coordination.

Step 3: Parallel Splitting

A key observation enables parallelism: split decisions at one node in the decision tree are unrelated to decisions at other nodes. This means the tree can be grown at different nodes in parallel.

Physical Layout

All rows remain in one large Spark DataFrame, partitioned across executors with no particular ordering. Each row logically belongs to some leaf node in the current (partially built) decision tree. Given the current tree structure and feature values, each worker can determine which leaf node owns each of its rows.

Handling Small Nodes (In-Memory Build)

When a leaf node has few enough rows to fit in one worker’s memory, the rows for that node are collected via a hash-partition exchange (shuffle) to a single executor. That executor then builds the entire subtree for that node using the fast in-memory algorithm. Once the data fits in memory, recursive splitting happens locally and the subtree is complete.

Handling Big Nodes (Distributed Build)

For nodes with too many rows to fit on one machine, PLANET avoids moving row data between machines. Instead:

  1. Each executor computes partial statistics for every candidate split (feature and threshold combination) using only its local partition of data
  2. Statistics include counts like left-no, left-yes, right-no, right-yes for each split option
  3. These small statistics tables are aggregated (summed) across all executors to form complete statistics for each node
  4. The driver uses the complete statistics to choose the best split for each node

Each statistics table corresponds to a decision tree node being split. Each column in the table represents a feature, and each row represents a threshold (bucket boundary). The best split is the one that maximizes impurity reduction.

After splitting, the process repeats: new leaf nodes are classified as either small enough for in-memory processing or still requiring the distributed approach. The algorithm continues recursively until all nodes reach a stopping condition.

Note

The critical insight of PLANET is that it shuffles statistics (small summary tables), not row data (potentially massive). This dramatically reduces network communication compared to sorting or redistributing the actual training data.

Conclusion

  • Machine learning models are functions that learn to predict outputs from inputs, with supervised learning being the most common paradigm
  • Data should be split into train, validation, and test sets to properly evaluate model performance and avoid overfitting
  • Spark MLlib uses an immutable API: estimators produce transformers via .fit(), and transformers add prediction columns via .transform()
  • Pipelines chain together transformers and estimators into a single reusable workflow
  • Decision trees make predictions through nested conditional splits on feature values, with impurity measures guiding split quality
  • Ensemble methods (random forests, gradient-boosted trees) combine many small trees for better predictions
  • Tree-based methods remain highly effective for structured/tabular data even in the deep learning era
  • The PLANET algorithm enables distributed decision tree training by using equi-depth histograms to define a fixed set of candidate split points, computing partial statistics in parallel, and aggregating them to choose optimal splits — all without shuffling the actual training data

ASIANAM 160: Asian American History

Course Details

Term: Fall 2024 · Instructor: (UW–Madison ASIANAM faculty) · Credits: 3 Meets: Monday/Wednesday/Friday

Description

A survey of Asian American history from the mid-19th century to the present, using immigration as the primary lens. The course traces Chinese, Japanese, South Asian, Filipino, Korean, Vietnamese, Hmong, and Cambodian immigration through cycles of recruitment, exploitation, exclusion, and eventual legal recognition — and examines how US foreign policy and racial ideology shaped each wave. The second half turns to literature and memoir (The Latehomecomer by Kao Kalia Yang) to recover histories that archives cannot hold. The throughline: Asian immigration is not marginal to US history — it is a window into globalization, labor, race, citizenship, and empire.
